pages.title: Part 1: Quantitative Versus Qualitative Analysis
pages.readingHtml:
Quantitative Analysis in Biomechanical Research

The biomechanical assessment of human movement generally falls into two distinct paradigms based on the nature of data collection, analytical techniques, and intended application: quantitative analysis and qualitative analysis. Biomechanists spend considerable effort devising objective techniques to measure specific physical variables that optimize human movement and athletic performance. When researchers collect numeric measurements of performance, they perform a quantitative analysis.

Quantitative analysis relies on high-tech laboratory instrumentation to capture precise physical metrics. These advanced toolkits include:

  • Computerized Force-Measuring Platforms (Force Plates): Transducers embedded in the floor or equipment that measure ground reaction forces (GRF), center of pressure (COP) drift, and rate of force development (RFD) during explosive actions such as a sprinter's starting block push-off or a vertical jump takeoff.
  • Electromyography (EMG): Surface or fine-wire intramuscular electrodes that detect electrical action potentials propagating across the sarcolemma, recording the timing, sequence, and relative magnitude of muscle activation during complex motor skills.
  • High-Speed Video Recording and Digitizing Systems: Multi-camera motion capture arrays operating at high frame rates (100 to 1000+ Hz) that track spatial coordinates of reflective anatomical markers, enabling computerized 3-D kinematic digitizing and joint angle calculation (e.g., analyzing segment velocities during a high jump).

Because quantitative methodology requires expensive equipment, rigorous calibration protocols, and specialized analytical expertise, it is primarily restricted to scientific research laboratories and elite sports science institutes.

Qualitative Analysis in Coaching and Pedagogy

In contrast to laboratory researchers, sports coaches, physical educators, and clinical practitioners rarely have immediate access to complex electronic digitizing equipment or force plates during daily practice. Instead, practitioners rely on sensory information—primarily visual observations and aural cues (e.g., sound of foot strike, rhythmic cadence)—to assess movement efficiency. This observational approach is defined as qualitative analysis.

A rigorous qualitative analysis is not merely an unguided guess; it requires a systematic four-part observational and diagnostic framework:

  1. Observational Framework: Establishing optimal viewing perspectives, distance, and environmental conditions from which skilled movement patterns can be systematically observed.
  2. Biomechanical Principles: Applying fundamental mechanical principles (e.g., impulse-momentum, lever mechanics, fluid resistance) to evaluate the movement pattern.
  3. Error Detection Checklist: Utilizing a structured mental or written checklist to identify biomechanical deviations, technical errors, and performance bottlenecks.
  4. Remediation and Feedback Techniques: Developing specific pedagogical instructions, physical drills, and corrective cues to help the athlete or patient rectify identified mechanical flaws.
Analytical ParameterQuantitative AnalysisQualitative Analysis
Primary Data TypeNumeric measurements (scalars and vectors)Descriptive sensory observations (visual/aural)
Primary InstrumentationForce plates, EMG, 3-D high-speed video captureHuman sight, hearing, systematic checklists
Primary Target AudienceBiomechanics researchers, clinical scientistsCoaches, physical educators, athletic trainers
Operational SettingControlled laboratory or instrumented field sitesDaily practice fields, courts, clinical gymnasiums
Primary FocusPrecise measurement of physical forces and anglesMovement pattern evaluation and technical correction
Clinical / Coaching Application

A track and field coach training a 100-m sprinter integrates qualitative analysis by observing the block start from a lateral perspective. Using a systematic checklist, the coach identifies an error: the sprinter's hip angle is too low at set position, preventing optimal extension. Rather than needing a $50,000 force plate array in real-time, the coach provides immediate verbal cues and technical adjustments. However, in an off-season biomechanics lab, quantitative force-plate digitizing may be used to measure the exact horizontal impulse (F · Δt) produced against each block pedal to validate the qualitative intervention.

pages.title: Part 2: Kinematics Versus Kinetics
pages.readingHtml:
Kinematics: Describing the Geometry of Motion

Mechanics is divided into two primary branches when studying movement: kinematics and kinetics. The study of kinematics describes the spatial and temporal (timing) characteristics of the motion of the human body and its segments, without any reference to the forces that cause or modify the movement. Kinematic analysis applies to both linear motion (translation) and angular motion (rotation), answering four fundamental questions about performance:

  • How long? Examining temporal variables such as movement duration (t), contact time, and stride frequency.
  • How far? Measuring spatial displacement (d) and total distance traveled.
  • How fast? Quantifying linear velocity (v), angular velocity (ω), and linear or angular speed.
  • How consistent? Assessing intra-individual variability and repeatability of movement trajectories across multiple trials.

Core kinematic variables include time (t), position/displacement (d), velocity (v = Δd / Δt), and acceleration (a = Δv / Δt). For example, calculating a sprinter's peak stride velocity (11.5 m/s) or a golfer's clubhead angular speed without measuring muscle forces represents a pure kinematic evaluation.

Kinetics: Analyzing Cause and Effect Forces

While kinematics describes what motion occurs, kinetics focuses on the underlying forces that cause, produce, or alter that movement. Quantifying forces enables biomechanists to determine the exact mechanical causes of movement because net forces induce mass acceleration according to Newton's second law (ΣF = m · a), which directly dictates velocity changes and spatial displacement.

Kinetics categorizes forces acting on the human system into two distinct classifications:

  1. Internal Forces: Forces generated within the biological system. These primarily include pulling forces generated by skeletal muscle contractions transmitted via tendinous insertions onto bone, as well as compressive and shear reaction forces exerted across joint articular cartilage (bone-on-bone forces).
  2. External Forces: Forces exerted on the human body by the external environment. Key external forces include gravitational attraction (Fg = m · g, where g ≈ 9.81 m/s2), ground reaction forces (GRF) exerted by the surface during contact, fluid resistance (hydrodynamic drag and lift in water or aerodynamic drag in air), and contact forces from sport equipment or opponents.
Biomechanical DomainKinematicsKinetics
Core DefinitionDescription of spatial and timing characteristics of motionAnalysis of forces that produce, modify, or cause motion
Core Questions AnsweredHow long? How far? How fast? How consistent?Why does the body move? What forces cause acceleration?
Primary VariablesTime (t), Displacement (d), Velocity (v), Acceleration (a)Force (F), Torque (τ), Mass (m), Pressure (P), Work/Energy
Force CategoriesN/A (Forces are completely ignored)Internal (muscles, tendons) and External (gravity, GRF, drag)
Practical ExampleMeasuring knee flexion angle (120°) during a jump landingMeasuring patellofemoral joint reaction force (6,000 N) during landing
Clinical / Coaching Application

In clinical gait rehabilitation following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction, physical therapists combine kinematics and kinetics to evaluate recovery. Kinematic camera tracking reveals if the patient exhibits diminished knee flexion range of motion (45° vs. 65° during stance phase). However, kinetic force-plate analysis reveals the underlying cause: the patient is under-loading the surgical limb, producing a ground reaction force of only 1.2 × body weight compared to 2.1 × body weight on the uninjured side. Correcting kinetic force distribution is essential to prevent secondary osteoarthritic changes.

pages.title: Part 3: Models of Human Motion and Center of Mass
pages.readingHtml:
Biomechanics and Simplified Spatial Models

Biomechanics is formally defined as the science that examines the internal and external forces acting on the human body and the biological effects produced by these forces. Analyzing human movement presents immense analytical challenges: all body tissues undergo shape deformations during vigorous physical activity, and human movement occurs across three spatial dimensions. To simplify complex movement dynamics, biomechanists employ three standardized modeling representations: the particle model, stick figure model, and rigid body segment model.

  • Particle Model: Replaces the entire body or object with a single mathematical point mass located at its center of mass. This simplified model is used exclusively when the body or object is airborne and acting as a projectile. Examples include airborne balls (thrown, struck, or kicked) and the human body in flight during diving, high jumping, gymnastics tumbling, or ski jumping.
  • Stick Figure Model: Represents athletes who are in contact with the ground or apparatus (e.g., diving board, starting block). Body segments are depicted as 2-D rigid bars (sticks) connected at joint pivot points. It effectively displays total body configuration, segment lengths, and external forces for gross motor skills occurring in two dimensions (e.g., sprint starts, running strides, somersaults). Limitations: It cannot easily represent fine localized muscle actions (e.g., hand grip on a bat) or 3-D longitudinal axial rotations.
  • Rigid Body Segment Model: The most sophisticated approach for 3-D motion analysis, representing each anatomical segment as an irregularly shaped 3-D volumetric solid. Used in advanced computer motion capture arrays to calculate 3-D joint torques, inertial properties, and multi-plane rotations.

Center of Mass Dynamics and Sex-Based Normative Differences

The single point around which a body's mass is equally distributed in all spatial directions is defined as the center of mass (also referred to as the center of gravity [CG]). For a perfectly symmetrical object of homogeneous density (such as a bowling ball or golf ball), the CG is located at its geometric center. For a homogeneous hollow ring (such as a ringette ring), the CG is located in the hollow space outside the physical material.

In the human body, the location of the CG is dynamic and depends on posture and body segment positions:

  • In standard anatomical standing position, the human CG is located approximately 6 inches above the groin area in the pelvic cavity.
  • Sex-Based Normative Data: Standing CG is located at approximately 55% of standing height in females and 57% of standing height in males.
  • Because females possess a broader pelvic structure and lower relative mass distribution, females generally exhibit a lower center of gravity than males, providing greater mechanical stability in balance tasks.

Projectile Parabolic Trajectory Principles

The location of the CG is of paramount biomechanical importance because a human body in flight behaves as though its entire mass were concentrated at this single point. Once a human athlete leaves the ground and becomes a projectile (such as during a long jump or high jump), the trajectory of the body's CG is strictly governed by gravity and follows an unalterable parabolic trajectory. No movement of limbs or body segments in mid-air can alter the parabolic path of the CG once airborne. However, athletes manipulate body segment orientation around the CG (e.g., the Fosbury flop in high jump or hitch-kick in long jump) to clear obstacles or maximize reach while the CG follows its predetermined parabolic path.

Biomechanical ModelSpatial DimensionSegment RepresentationPrimary Athletic ApplicationKey Limitations
Particle Model1-D / 2-D / 3-D PointSingle dot at Center of MassAirborne projectiles (diving, balls, high jump)Ignores segment rotations and limb posture
Stick Figure Model2-D Planar SurfaceRigid bars connected at joint pivotsGround-contact skills (sprint start, running)Cannot show 3-D axial rotations or fine grip
Rigid Body ModelFull 3-D Spatial VolumeIrregular 3-D volumetric solidsComplex 3-D skills (golf swing, pitching, gymnastics)Requires high-end computer capture arrays
Clinical / Coaching Application

In the high jump, the development of the Fosbury flop technique revolutionized the sport through clever application of center of mass principles. By arching the back over the crossbar in a belly-up position, the athlete redistributes head and leg mass downward on either side of the bar. Consequently, the athlete's Center of Gravity (CG) actually passes beneath or through the crossbar while the physical body successfully clears the height! Understanding that the airborne CG follows a fixed parabolic arc enables coaches to teach optimal bar clearance mechanics without requiring impossible vertical impulse increases.

glossary.def: The objective measurement and numerical evaluation of biomechanical performance variables using scientific instrumentation such as force plates, electromyography, and motion capture systems.
The non-numerical observation and visual/aural evaluation of human movement quality using a systematic framework of principles, checklists, and corrective feedback.
The branch of biomechanics that describes the spatial and temporal characteristics of motion (time, displacement, velocity, acceleration) without regard to the forces causing the movement.
The branch of biomechanics that analyzes the internal and external forces that cause, produce, or modify the motion of a biological system.
Forces generated within the biological system, primarily muscular pulling forces transmitted via tendons to bones and joint reaction forces across articular surfaces.
Forces acting on the human body from the outside environment, including gravity, ground reaction forces, fluid resistance, and contact from equipment or opponents.
The science that examines the internal and external forces acting on the human body and the biological effects produced by these forces.
A simplified biomechanical model that represents the total body or object as a single point mass at its center of mass, used primarily for airborne projectiles.
A 2-D biomechanical model that represents body segments as rigid bars connected at joint pivot points, used for analyzing ground-contact gross motor skills.
A sophisticated 3-D biomechanical model that represents each body segment as an irregularly shaped 3-D volume for detailed multi-planar motion analysis.
The single balance point around which a body's total mass is equally distributed in all directions; also termed center of gravity (CG).
An airborne body or object that is propelled into the air and affected only by the forces of gravity and fluid/air resistance.
